name: Manitoba
overview: Manitoba sits at the geographic centre of Canada. Most of its post-secondary institutions are in Winnipeg, a mid-sized city with a strong arts scene and a large French-speaking community in St. Boniface. Brandon offers a smaller-city alternative in the province's southwest.
highlights: A mix of universities, colleges and a polytechnic, concentrated in Winnipeg
French-language post-secondary study is available in St. Boniface
Very cold winters and warm summers — budget for proper winter clothing
The province runs its own nominee program with streams for graduates; check the official site for current criteria

name: Ontario
overview: Ontario is Canada's most populous province and home to the largest number of universities and colleges. Options range from large research universities in the Greater Toronto Area to smaller campuses in mid-sized cities, where living costs can be noticeably lower.
highlights: The widest choice of institutions and programs in the country
Large, diverse international student communities
Housing costs vary widely between Toronto and smaller cities
Ottawa offers bilingual (English/French) study options

name: British Columbia
overview: British Columbia combines Pacific coastline and mountains with a well-known university and college system. Metro Vancouver is a major hub for international students, while the Okanagan and Vancouver Island offer smaller-city campus life.
highlights: Milder coastal winters than most of Canada
Strong technology, film and natural resource sectors
Housing in Metro Vancouver is among the most expensive in Canada
Outdoor recreation close to most campuses

name: Alberta
overview: Alberta's two largest cities, Calgary and Edmonton, host major universities and polytechnics. The province is known for energy, agriculture and a growing technology sector, and the Rocky Mountains are a short drive from Calgary.
highlights: Polytechnics with strong applied and trades programs
No provincial sales tax
Cold, dry winters with sunny days
Close to Banff and Jasper national parks

name: Québec
overview: Québec is Canada's predominantly French-speaking province, with both French- and English-language universities and a distinct college system (CEGEPs). Montréal is a lively, multilingual university city.
highlights: French is the official language; some institutions teach in English
A distinct college (CEGEP) system
Rich cultural life and festivals
Québec runs its own selection process for students and immigrants
specialNote: Students going to Québec generally need a Québec Acceptance Certificate (CAQ) from the Québec government in addition to a federal study permit. Check the Québec government's current requirements before you apply.

name: Saskatchewan
overview: Saskatchewan offers university and polytechnic study in Saskatoon and Regina, with a lower cost of living than Canada's largest cities. Agriculture, mining and research are important parts of the economy.
highlights: Generally lower housing costs than large metro areas
Strengths in agriculture and resource-related research
Very cold winters, sunny climate
A provincial nominee program with options for graduates

name: Nova Scotia
overview: Nova Scotia has a high number of universities for its size, many of them in Halifax. Coastal life, a historic port city and close-knit campus communities are part of the appeal.
highlights: Several universities within one compact city (Halifax)
Ocean sciences and marine-related programs
Milder winters than the Prairies, with plenty of snow and wind
Small-town campus options outside Halifax

name: New Brunswick
overview: New Brunswick is Canada's only officially bilingual province. It offers English- and French-language universities and colleges in small to mid-sized cities with an affordable cost of living.
highlights: Officially bilingual (English and French)
Smaller class sizes at many institutions
Lower living costs than large metro areas
Atlantic coastline and forests

name: Newfoundland and Labrador
overview: Canada's most easterly province is known for its rugged coastline, friendly communities and distinctive culture. Post-secondary study is centred in St. John's, with additional campuses elsewhere in the province.
highlights: Strong ocean, fisheries and energy-related programs
Distinctive local culture and music
Windy, changeable maritime weather
Smaller student population and close community feel

name: Prince Edward Island
overview: Canada's smallest province offers a quiet, community-oriented study experience, mainly in Charlottetown. It is well known for its beaches, farmland and food.
highlights: Small, walkable capital city
Programs connected to agriculture, food and island industries
Seasonal tourism economy
Short travel distances across the province

name: Yukon
overview: Yukon is a northern territory with vast wilderness and a small population. Post-secondary options are limited and centred in Whitehorse, with a focus on northern and applied programs.
highlights: Northern and Indigenous-focused learning
Long summer daylight, very long winter nights
Small, close-knit communities
Higher costs for some goods due to remoteness

name: Northwest Territories
overview: The Northwest Territories offers a small number of post-secondary programs, many with a northern or Indigenous focus. Yellowknife is the territorial capital.
highlights: Northern lights viewing for much of the year
Programs linked to northern communities and resources
Extreme cold in winter
Remote location affects travel and living costs

name: Nunavut
overview: Nunavut is Canada's largest and most northern territory. Post-secondary study is limited and closely tied to the needs of Inuit communities.
highlights: Inuit culture and languages
Community-based learning
Arctic climate
Access is mainly by air
